extracted.intended_audience: comedy fans and performers, and general readers interested in viral comedy culture
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria for judging stand-up crowd work/heckler interactions and viral 'heckler destroyed' clips — distinguishing genuine, skillful audience-handling from manufactured, attention-seeking conflict. Useful for critics, comedians, and viewers assessing quality and ethics of such bits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality of the comic's verbal response (parrying vs attention-seeking)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the comedian is 'reacting to an unruly audience member and parrying their outbursts with perfect clap-backs' versus merely seeking attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page contrasts skillful, on-the-spot rebuttals ('perfect clap-backs') with 'desperate instigator' behavior—comics who barrage a target with insults not to be funny but to get a reaction. Good crowd work should look like genuine repartee, not a one-sided attention grab.

rubrics_metrics.name: Material quality: jokes versus cries for attention
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguishes 'Not quite jokes. More like cries for attention.' — material that functions as actual joke-writing versus material meant only to provoke or be photographed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the interaction reads as attention-seeking rather than composed jokes, it's judged poor. Strong crowd work relies on comedic content, not theatrical baiting for clicks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity of the conflict (spontaneous vs manufactured)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the moment of confrontation is spontaneous or a manufactured moment of conflict created by the comic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article warns that many performers 'manufacture moments of conflict with audience members who might not take the bait' to satisfy posting schedules and platform algorithms. Authentic crowd work should feel unscripted and not like staged provocation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honesty/accuracy about what the crowd said or did
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoiding fabrication: 'You know your crowd work is terrible when you have to make up the things said by the crowd.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presenting invented audience lines or fabricating confrontation is an anti-pattern and signals poor crowd-work practice; credibility suffers when comics invent crowd responses to create drama.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of target and power dynamics (punching down)
rubrics_metrics.description: Who the comic singles out (e.g., 'a quiet, unamused woman') and whether the interaction targets someone unlikely to fight back.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Targeting an unbothered or vulnerable audience member for provocation is framed as crass and unfunny; good crowd work should avoid exploiting power imbalances for cheap laughs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Performer ethics and reputation
rubrics_metrics.description: Context about the comic's past conduct (e.g., previous incidents like being 'booted from a bunch of shows' or cheering violence) that affects judgment of their crowd work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article suggests a performer's prior behavior and ethical stance (such as endorsing harmful acts) matter when evaluating their actions onstage; dubious pasts can make crowd work feel worse or more problematic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algorithmic motives versus artistic merit
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognition that 'the algorithms of every content platform reward crowd work clips, and, specifically, "heckler destruction" videos,' which can distort performers' motives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique should account for whether a bit exists for art/comedy or for virality; chasing algorithmic rewards by manufacturing confrontations is presented as a negative force shaping modern crowd work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Success defined by provocation versus comedic skill
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguishing success measured by generating outrage/virality ('that sweet, clickable outrage') from success measured by actual comedic skill and material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article highlights that virality (views/ratios) is not equivalent to good comedy; an interaction can be widely shared yet be a 'colossal self-own' if it fails as comedy and exists mainly to provoke.
